name: LEXICON
expansion: Lexical Encoding of eXperiment Information as Checked Observable tokeNs

intro.problem: Detector events are treated as vectors of continuous features, and the co-occurrence tools that let language models learn structure [@levy2014] have barely been tried on whether events carry a grammar of their own; the closest precedent tokenizes whole events for anomaly detection [@visive2025].
intro.value: If they do, a token model trained only on background could score how typical an event is, giving a new axis for a data-driven background estimate, and token embeddings could become a new kind of classifier input, as tokenized jets already have [@finke2023][@birk2024].
intro.approach: Each feature is quantized with evidence-based edges [@scargle2013], so an event becomes a set of tokens. Route A1 fits density models to background and uses their surprise as an ABCD axis; Route A2 fits them to signal; Route A3 splits the signal-to-background likelihood ratio [@neyman1933] into what tokens carry alone and through their relations [@chowliu1968]; Route B trains classifiers.
intro.goals: The goal is a fair verdict on whether tokens add information beyond the raw features, with each token axis built only from the features of the network it replaces. Confirmation runs under frozen rules decide the background-only axis; comparing signal and background models decides whether events have a grammar that separates them.

questions: Does co-occurrence among binned detector features carry signal-versus-background information beyond the raw values?
Does an exact likelihood make background surprise a better ABCD axis than a pseudo-likelihood?
When signal and background token models are compared, do the relations between tokens separate the two beyond what the tokens carry one at a time?

tagline: Detector events as tokens: does an event have a grammar?

components.name: Route A1
components.subtitle: Background-only surprise as an ABCD axis
components.summary: Token models trained on background alone (this was Route A before the split) score how surprising each event is, and that score replaces one network as an axis of the ABCD plane. Signal labels and network scores never enter the token models, and each model sees only the features of the network it replaces, so the axis can be independent of the other. Two such models, one per network, also give a plane with no labels on either axis.

items.label: Independence
items.detail: Product of per-feature marginals: the floor every other model must beat

items.label: Pairs and triples
items.detail: Count models over feature pairs and triples; the best model in the data-starved barrel

items.label: CutFormer
items.detail: Masked-token transformer with feature-ID embeddings and no positions [@golling2024]; the best model in the endcap

items.label: Evt2Vec
items.detail: Skip-gram token embeddings [@levy2014] as a comparison

components.name: Route A1 variant
components.subtitle: Exact likelihood
components.summary: The transformer's pseudo-likelihood is not a normalized density and undercounts redundant features that predict each other. An autoregressive model gives an exact negative log-likelihood by the chain rule, which holds for any feature order, so the ordering that rules recurrence out of a classifier is legitimate for a density. Status: the variants and a pre-registered evaluation are written down and under review; nothing has run yet. Runs start in the barrel, and only variants that pass there go on to the endcap.

items.label: Exact count models
items.detail: Tree and small-graph models of pair counts: an exact likelihood with no training seed

items.label: MADE
items.detail: Masked autoregressive MLP [@germain2015]; set aside for a model that shares weights across orders, kept as a control

items.label: Any-order CutFormer
items.detail: Same transformer trained over random orders, giving an exact likelihood averaged across them

items.label: GRU
items.detail: Background-only recurrent density over a fixed feature order [@cho2014], within one network's features; kept because barrel runs are cheap, always read beside the other exact models

items.label: Order ensemble
items.detail: Several random orderings averaged, with their spread as a per-event uncertainty [@uria2014]

items.label: Gates
items.detail: Per-feature sigmoid gates showing which features carry the surprise; deferred

components.name: Route A2
components.subtitle: Signal token models
components.summary: Fit the same token models to signal, read through the edges fitted on background so both use one vocabulary and no label enters the tokenizer. Asks whether signal has a structure of its own, whether it holds across the signal hypotheses, and where signal sits among background's tokens. It uses labels, so it is not background-only, and its tokens are audited for simulation-versus-data artifacts before anything is claimed.

items.label: Same ladder
items.detail: Independence, pair and triple counts, a tree model with an exact likelihood [@chowliu1968], and the transformer where signal statistics allow

items.label: Signal statistics
items.detail: Few signal events per hypothesis: pool them with the hypothesis as a conditioning token, or fine-tune from the background model

items.label: Occupancy
items.detail: Where signal lands in background's vocabulary; the tokens it fills that background rarely does become the audit list

components.name: Route A3
components.subtitle: Signal against background
components.summary: Compare the signal and background models. Their log-likelihood ratio is the optimal discriminant when the densities are right [@neyman1933]; for tree models it splits exactly into a marginal term, what each token carries alone, and a relational term, what the relations between tokens carry. Whether the relational term adds separation is the most direct test of whether events have a grammar. The same comparison shows where the networks' information comes from and which relations cross the split between the two networks.

items.label: Grammar contrast
items.detail: Pair by pair, how much more or less two tokens co-occur in signal than in background, with a false-discovery control and replication on new folds

items.label: Exact decomposition
items.detail: Marginal plus relational terms on a tree skeleton chosen from background alone [@chowliu1968]

items.label: Ratio as an axis
items.detail: Built per network feature set and tested for closure like any network score; it is supervised, not background-only

components.name: Route B
components.subtitle: Supervised on tokens
components.summary: Use the labels with discriminative models on tokens: a linear read-out of the tokens, a probe on the background model's embeddings, a fine-tuned transformer, and embeddings into a small network. The generative form, a likelihood ratio between signal and background token densities, is now Route A3.

items.label: Audit first
items.detail: Check tokens that appear only in signal for simulation-versus-data artifacts before trusting them

items.label: No recurrent classifier
items.detail: A recurrent network imposes an order on features that have none; as a density that is harmless, as a classifier it is not, so it is not used here

components.name: Route C
components.subtitle: Tokens into the networks
components.summary: Feed token or event embeddings to the existing networks as inputs; per-event pooled vectors are where the value is expected to be.

results.title: First comparisons are a baseline
results.text: Summed surprise was first built from every feature, so it shared inputs with the network it was paired with. In the barrel it closed often but carried little signal; in the endcap it came about as close to closure as the regularized network pairs while keeping less signal in the signal region. Because of the shared inputs, neither result is a fair test; both are being rerun with separated features.

results.title: Background tokens predict each other
results.text: Co-occurrence structure is real and large in both regions, mostly through pairs. In the barrel, simple pair-and-triple counts beat the transformer on every seed; in the endcap, the larger sample lets the transformer go further.

results.title: Tokenizing is cheap
results.text: Coarse binning in the barrel loses only a small share of the raw-value context information; finer bins starve for events.

results.title: Signal information cancels in the sum
results.text: Individual tokens carry signal information in both directions, so summing surprise over features cancels it, which is why total surprise is a weak classifier.

results.title: Bin edges matter in the tail
results.text: An open top quantile bin hides the signal tail; evidence-based edges split it and move signal onto rare tokens [@scargle2013].

results.title: Not yet a measurement
results.text: Comparisons are single-seed, use the wide first-round network sweep rather than the refined models, and pick the surprise sign after seeing data; the separated-feature runs come first, then multiple seeds.

open.text: A recurrent model (GRU) is used only as a density: the chain rule holds for any feature order, so an exact likelihood is legitimate, but as a classifier it would impose an order on features that have none. It appears in Routes A1, A2 and A3 as a density or a ratio of densities, with several random orders averaged, and not in Route B or as a network input encoder.
